title: When the Lantern Breaks
premise: In the waning months of a devastating continental war, Quentin Vane serves as a battlefield nurse in a mobile hospital, secretly keeping a ledger of the wounded and dead whose names the officers' reports omit—deserters, colonial conscripts, women in disguise, the poor. When a census taker named Ada Brannock arrives to count the living, her one question too many forces Quentin to realize his ledger is evidence, not just grief. As victors' historians arrive to write a clean official record, Quentin and Ada race to get the true names on the public record before the archives are sealed. In the end, Quentin testifies at great personal cost, loses his anonymity but gains a found family among those he counted, and the ledger enters the archive under every name it holds—including, finally, his own.
about_author: Wren Kavanagh is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing wartime field records in provincial libraries. They write historical fiction about the people history tried not to count.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Quentin Vane's POV. Opening in a flooded field hospital, Quentin triages the wounded while memorizing names the officers' morning report omits—a colonial drummer boy, a deserter shot at dawn. At night he begins writing them in a small ledger. Emotional beat: quiet defiance born of exhaustion; establishes his rule that everything must fit in what can be carried.

chapters.title: The Census Taker
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Ada Brannock arrives with government papers to count the hospital's living. She asks each patient their full name and birthplace; when she reaches Quentin, she asks where he was born—and he realizes he has spent years answering nothing at all. Emotional beat: unease sharpening into recognition that invisibility is a choice he may no longer be allowed.

chapters.title: Names Omitted
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada compares her census sheets against the officers' casualty reports and finds dozens missing—the same names Quentin carries. She confronts him gently; he denies nothing and shows her three pages. Emotional beat: wary alliance forming between two people whose jobs are officially supposed to look away.

chapters.title: The Historians Arrive
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. A victory commission sweeps through: medals, photographs, a tidy narrative for the capital's archives. Colonel Ashe orders all unofficial paperwork surrendered for 'consolidation.' Quentin hides the ledger inside a crate of bandages. Emotional beat: dread; the machinery of official memory begins erasing what he has kept.

chapters.title: Sister Maren's Testimony
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The hospital's matron, Sister Maren, reveals she once testified after an earlier war and was ruined for it—dismissed, unemployable, erased. She warns them both but then, unexpectedly, offers Quentin the name of a sympathetic clerk in the provincial archive. Emotional beat: grief tempered by solidarity across generations.

chapters.title: One Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Under questioning from the commission, Quentin is asked directly whether any records exist outside official channels. He lies—and the lie costs him sleep, and nearly costs him the trust of a wounded soldier whose brother's name is in the ledger. Emotional beat: guilt crystallizing into resolve; lying to protect the truth no longer works.

chapters.title: The Long Road to the Archive
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Quentin, Ada, and the clerk's courier move the ledger by cart through checkpoints toward the provincial capital while Ashe's adjutant follows rumors of 'a nurse with a book.' A near-discovery at a river crossing forces Ada to memorize pages in case the ledger is lost. Emotional beat: rising tension; the stakes become physical and shared.

chapters.title: Ashes of the Morning Report
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Back at the hospital, Ashe discovers the empty crate and burns the remaining unofficial papers as a warning, demoting Quentin to laundry duty. Sister Maren publicly takes responsibility, sacrificing herself so Quentin can stay free. Emotional beat: climax of loss; the cost of the record becomes personal and irreversible.

chapters.title: On the Record
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. In the provincial archive, Quentin gives sworn testimony, reading the ledger aloud name by name while the commission's lawyers object and historians take notes they cannot retract. The clerk enters the ledger into the permanent collection. Emotional beat: catharsis; grief transformed into public fact, voice steady through every name.

chapters.title: Every Name It Holds
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, epilogue-like. A year later, Quentin visits the archive where the ledger rests open in a display case; visitors search its pages for their own dead. Ada finds him there, and Sister Maren's name has been added to the record too. Quentin adds his own name last. Emotional beat: resolution; inheritance, identity, and found family secured on paper at last.
